description: We are a team of passionate and innovative students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. With a strong interest in AI, machine learning, and space technology, we aim to develop creative, data-driven solutions to real-world challenges using NASA’s open data. Our goal is to combine our technical skills, creativity, and collaborative spirit to build impactful solutions that contribute to a better understanding of Earth and space.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective turns NASA's Earth records into answers anyone can understand. Pick any place on a 3D globe and a question (is it getting hotter, drier, hazier, greener? is the groundwater running out?). The app plots NASA's record for that place and runs the Mann-Kendall significance test with Sen's slope. It then says in plain words whether the change is real or could be chance, and how fast it is happening per decade.

It covers all five steps of the challenge on one screen: variable, region, period, time series and significance. It works for any place on Earth through live NASA POWER data. An AI detective answers open questions by pulling real NASA data: 282 POWER parameters, GRACE groundwater, and about 1,000 satellite layers from NASA GIBS. It paints heat maps of where things are changing directly on the globe. Every number it states is checked back against the NASA data it fetched.

Proving that a change is real usually takes a scientist. We built this so that students, farmers, journalists and policymakers can do it themselves, with evidence instead of opinion.
details:
What it does Earth Trend Detective answers one question for any place on Earth: is this really changing, or is it chance? You choose a measure (temperature, rainfall, vegetation, air haze, drought, groundwater, sea ice, sea level), a place (about 40 preset regions, or any place you type) and a period (any range of years, optionally one season). The app shows the yearly record, a trend line, warming stripes and then-vs-now satellite maps on a 3D globe. A plain verdict says how fast it is changing per decade and whether the change is "very likely real" (p < 0.05) or "could be chance".

How it works

  • Statistics: the Mann-Kendall test (non-parametric, robust to outliers) decides significance, and Sen's slope measures the rate. Values are compared year to year or season to season, so the seasonal cycle can't fake a trend. A correlation view shows which measures move together. It removes the seasonal cycle and trends first, corrects for autocorrelation and checks for delayed effects.
  • Any place on Earth: OpenStreetMap supplies the place's outline, a grid of points is laid inside it, and each point is fetched live from NASA POWER and averaged.
  • AI detective: a LangGraph agent with about 20 tools.
    • It searches NASA POWER's catalogue of 282 parameters by meaning.
    • It scans whole regions cell by cell for significant trends.
    • It reads GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage, clipped to real borders.
    • It measures any of about 1,000 NASA GIBS satellite layers by decoding each map's colour palette back into real values.
    • Results stream onto the globe as live heat maps and satellite overlays.
    • A verification step traces every number in the answer back to the NASA data, and shows any number that doesn't match.
  • Interaction: voice questions and spoken answers (offline Whisper and Piper), steering the globe by hand through the webcam (MediaPipe), and a PDF report of any investigation.

Benefits and impact Trend analysis normally needs scientific software and statistics training. This makes it a 10-second question for students, teachers, farmers, journalists and local officials. Every answer shows its evidence and says honestly when a change could be chance, which helps fight both alarmism and denial.

Tools and languages TypeScript, Next.js 16 and React; CesiumJS for the 3D globe; LangGraph and LangChain for the AI agent; MediaPipe for hand tracking; Python with Whisper and Piper for voice; hand-written SVG charts plus bklit charts; h5py and NumPy for processing GRACE NetCDF data.

What makes it creative

  • It turns NASA's satellite map images back into measurements, so any of about 1,000 layers can be trend-tested.
  • An AI that cannot invent numbers: every figure is verified against NASA data.
  • Analysis made visible: the globe flies to each area the AI reads and paints where things are changing.

Factors we considered

  • Statistical honesty: non-parametric tests, the p < 0.05 rule from the challenge brief, and autocorrelation corrections.
  • Data resolution: the app says when a measurement is regional (about 50 km), and uses 1 km satellite land temperature for cities.
  • Offline reliability: the core analysis runs from local NASA files.
  • Plain language for a public audience: every technical term has an explanation.
